claim: The requirement asks for all generated code to carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage, and allows conditional emission only where the attribute does not exist. Every template wraps the attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. But `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it is valid on classes. So projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework get generated formatters and resolvers with no attribute, and the 'all generated code' criterion is not met for those targets. L7 records no preference and says to follow the requirement.

claim: A user who already wrote [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their own partial resolver declaration (for example `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver][ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] partial class MyResolver {}`, which is the obvious manual workaround for this issue) no longer compiles. The template does not check whether the user's declaration already carries the attribute. The same applies to user-declared `[CompositeResolver]` partial classes, via CompositeResolverTemplate.

claim: The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard drops the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it allows AttributeTargets.Class on those targets (only the Assembly target was added later). The guard is therefore unnecessary, and generated code on those targets is still counted in coverage, against 'all generated code is decorated'. Ledger L7 says to follow the requirement.

claim: The TransformUtilities change from "{" to "{\r\n" for nesting types with constraints is a behavior change with no dedicated test. The new tests use only non-nested, non-generic types, so negating or reverting the line would not fail them. Only snapshots could catch it, and only if a snapshot covers a nested generic type with constraints.

The guard test only accepts "#if
	[attr]
#endif
" or the unindented form. It never compiles the generated output with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK defined, and never compiles against a target framework where the attribute is absent. The guard symbols are therefore unverified as actually preventing a compile error. A wrong symbol such as a typo would still pass as long as the Guard constant in the test is the same typo.
